title: Set and Version a Threshold Policy
scenario: It is 6:25 AM. Before the risk and approval steps can run, Meridian needs an agreed set of thresholds - written down once, owned, and versioned - so no downstream step hardcodes its own business rules.
input: Meridian's risk desk has agreed how price movement on the ERCOT hub should be treated. A day-over-day move of 5% or more is a routine variance the morning brief should note. A move of 12% or more must be escalated for manager approval before the brief is sent. The policy is owned by the Risk Desk Lead and changes require sign-off from the Desk Manager. Record this as version 1.0.0.
instructions: Read the policy brief and note the agreed thresholds.
Set routineThreshold and escalationThreshold as numbers (percent, no % sign).
Record the policy owner and the required approver.
Set a version so future changes can be tracked.
Make sure escalation is greater than routine, then validate.
copilotPrompt: Draft a JSON threshold policy with policyName, version, owner, approver, routineThreshold, and escalationThreshold. Use plain numbers for the thresholds (no % sign) and make the escalation threshold higher than the routine threshold.
successMessage: Threshold policy set and versioned. Downstream risk and approval steps can now reuse these rules instead of hardcoding them.

intro.heading: Before you build: governance as config

sections.title: Config-as-rules
sections.body: Automation should not bury business rules inside code. When a threshold lives in a config object, the people who own the rule can read and change it without touching the workflow logic.

sections.title: What a threshold policy is
sections.body: A threshold policy names the values that decide when something matters - here, how big a price move is routine versus when it must be escalated. Writing it down once means every downstream step applies the same rule.

sections.title: Versioning and ownership
sections.body: A governed policy records who owns it, who approves changes, and which version is in force. That is what makes a rule auditable: you can see what changed, when, and who signed off.

sections.title: Why governance comes before automation acts
sections.body: Risk Evaluation, Approval Decision, and the Morning Brief all read these thresholds. If the policy is wrong or unowned, every step downstream inherits the mistake. Governance is set first so automation can act safely.

realWorld.soloRebuildPath: You'd write the threshold rules down in a shared doc or a config tab (e.g. 'flag if move > 8%') so the check reads one source of truth, not memory.

takeaway.heading: Threshold policy set
points: You turned a written policy brief into a versioned, owned threshold policy object.
The thresholds now live as config-as-rules, not hardcoded logic, so the owner can change them safely.
This policy sits in Phase 3, the Evaluation Layer, of the Meridian workflow map.
Risk Evaluation, Approval Decision, and the Morning Brief all reuse these same thresholds downstream.
The workflow can now apply consistent business thresholds without hardcoding rules.
